opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The first thing I'd say is that there's no such thing as a generic "safe" model. Risk is always tied to a specific application, its users, and the domain it operates in. So when a team at Bloomberg comes to us with a new generative AI product, we don't start from a general-purpose safety checklist. We start by asking what this system is supposed to do, who will use it, and what could go wrong in that particular setting.

A lot of the public conversation and existing taxonomies focus on harms that matter for consumer chatbots, like toxicity, hate speech, or someone asking how to build a weapon. Those matter, but in financial services the risks that keep us up at night look different. Is the system giving something that reads like financial advice? Could it leak confidential or material non-public information? Could it misrepresent what a company said on an earnings call, or produce content that looks like market manipulation? Is it being impartial in how it presents information? Those are domain-specific risks that general safety benchmarks and off-the-shelf guardrails mostly miss.

So our process looks roughly like this. First we build an application-specific risk taxonomy with the product team, our legal and compliance colleagues, and domain experts, because they know the regulatory landscape and failure modes far better than a generic framework would. Then we turn that taxonomy into concrete tests. That includes red teaming, both manual, by people who understand the domain and can probe edge cases creatively, and more automated, scaled-up adversarial testing. We also try to be realistic about the threat model. Not everyone using a terminal product is an adversary, so we test benign users who might be accidentally misled as well as people actively trying to break the system.

Another key point is that you can't evaluate the model in isolation. What matters is the whole system: retrieval, prompts, guardrails, the interface, how outputs are displayed and attributed. A model that behaves fine on its own might fail once you plug in a retrieval component that surfaces the wrong document. So we test end to end as much as possible.

And finally, it's not a one-time gate before launch. Models get updated, usage patterns shift, and people find new ways to interact with the system, so we treat risk assessment as ongoing, with monitoring and re-evaluation built into the product lifecycle. The overall philosophy is to be specific and grounded rather than relying on general claims that a model is "aligned" or "safe," because those claims rarely transfer cleanly to a real deployment in a specialized domain like finance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the first thing I'd say is that we don't really start with the model. We start with the application. A lot of the conversation around AI safety and red-teaming happens at the level of the foundation model, which makes sense if you're the one training it, but at Bloomberg we're mostly building products on top of models, and the risks that matter are very specific to what the product is actually supposed to do and who's using it.

So the way we approach it is we sit down and ask, what is this thing for, who is going to use it, and what does failure look like in this context? A summarization tool for earnings calls has a very different risk profile than a chat interface that a client might use to ask questions about market data. For one of them, the worst case might be a hallucinated number that gets into someone's research. For the other, it might be the system giving something that sounds like investment advice, which we're not in the business of doing and which has real regulatory implications. Those are not the same test suite.

Once we have that picture, we build out a taxonomy of the harms that are relevant to that application. Some of it is the general stuff you'd expect, toxicity, bias, prompt injection, and we do test for all of that. But the piece I think is underappreciated is the domain-specific risk. In finance there's a whole category of things that are not harmful in a general sense but are absolutely unacceptable in our context. Things like confidential information leaking across clients, the model speculating about mergers or price movements, or presenting something uncertain as established fact. A general-purpose safety benchmark is not going to catch most of that.

Then on the testing side, we use a mix of approaches. We have automated evaluation where we can, with curated datasets and adversarial prompts that we've built up over time, and we use models to help generate and grade a lot of that at scale. But we also do a lot of human red-teaming, and we deliberately bring in people from different parts of the company, not just the ML team. The people who understand the product, the compliance folks, people who know what a journalist or an analyst would actually try to do. They find things we would never think of, because they know the domain and they know the users.

One thing I've learned is that this really has to be a continuous process rather than a gate you pass through once. Models change, the application changes, and the way people use it changes once it's out in the world. So we try to build the evaluation into the development cycle so that every time something is updated, the same battery of tests runs again, and we keep adding to it based on what we see in production.

And I'd say the last thing, which is maybe a bit philosophical, is that we try to be honest about what testing can and can't tell us. You can never prove a generative system is safe. What you can do is build enough evidence that you understand its failure modes well enough to deploy it responsibly, with the right guardrails and the right monitoring around it. The testing is one input into that decision, not a certificate.

r001.rationale: It says risk assessment starts with the application’s purpose, users, and context, and gives different tests for different intended user experiences.

r002.rationale: It explains that people beyond the ML team, who understand the domain and users, find risks the team would otherwise miss.

r003.rationale: It says product, compliance, and domain-aware staff take part in human red-teaming, but does not clearly say they help develop the risk test plans.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with the application rather than the model in isolation. What is the user trying to do, what information does the model have access to, and what happens if it gets something wrong? Those questions help you identify which risks you need to test.

For example, if you’re summarizing a financial document, a summary can sound very fluent but get a number wrong or leave out a qualification that changes the meaning. So you want to evaluate whether the claims are supported by the document, not just whether the output reads well.

Then I’d involve domain experts in building realistic test cases, including cases where the system should acknowledge that it doesn’t have enough information. You can automate some of that evaluation, but human judgment is important for understanding the consequences of an error. And testing needs to continue as the application changes—you don’t establish that a system is safe with one benchmark score.

r001.rationale: It says to identify risks based on what the user is trying to do, but does not clearly state that risk categories should be prioritized according to the intended client experience.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss AI engineers conducting red teaming or how their experience could skew test queries.

r003.rationale: It explicitly recommends involving domain experts in building realistic test cases for evaluating the application’s risks.

sol-6.1.text:
We start with the use case, because the risks depend on what the application is doing and how someone is going to use its output. If it summarizes a financial document, for example, what happens if it gets a number wrong, leaves out an important qualification, or makes a claim that isn’t supported by the source?

Then we turn those potential failures into test cases. We want representative examples, but also difficult cases where we think the system might break. And we need domain experts involved, because a response can sound very fluent and still contain a consequential error that a general-purpose metric won’t catch.

The other piece is testing the whole application, rather than just the model. What information does it retrieve? How is that information presented to the model? Can the user check the sources? Those choices affect the risk. So the goal is to build evidence that the system is reliable enough for its intended use, understand where it falls short, and keep evaluating it as it changes.
